name: Visual Genome
description: Visual Genome is a dataset connecting language and vision using crowdsourced dense image annotations. It contains over 100K images where each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. The dataset includes region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases are canonicalized to WordNet synsets. The dataset contains 1,773,258 question-answer pairs and over 4 million region descriptions.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei
citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., and Fei-Fei, L. Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations.
rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation. Approximately 800,000 Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs) were launched on AMT, where each HIT involved creating descriptions, questions and answers, or region graphs. Each HIT was designed such that workers earn anywhere between $6-$8 per hour. The dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M and MS-COCO datasets.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from the intersection of MS-COCO (328,000 images) and YFCC100M (100 million images). These are real-world, non-iconic images uploaded onto Flickr by users. The images range from as small as 72 pixels wide to as large as 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: 6 months of data collection after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and question-answer pairs are canonicalized to WordNet synsets. Stanford NLP tools are used to extract noun phrases. Attributes are normalized based on morphology (stemming). Hand-crafted mapping rules are applied for common failure cases (30 rules for objects, 15 for attributes, 20 for relationships). Objects from different region graphs with bounding box overlap over union of 0.8 are merged. BLEU score thresholds of 0.7 are used to ensure diversity in region descriptions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Region descriptions are preprocessed by removing all non-alphanumeric characters, lowercasing, and stripping excess whitespace. For attribute and relationship experiments, data is lowercased, lemmatized, and stripped of excess whitespace. Objects are extracted using Stanford's dependency parser combined with crowdsourcing. BLEU score thresholds are used to prevent duplicate region descriptions. For scene graph construction, objects with bounding box intersection over union of 0.8 are merged, verified by workers. For canonicalization, noun phrases are mapped to most frequent matching WordNet synsets, refined by hand-crafted rules and verified by AMT workers.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were collected through multiple crowdsourcing stages on Amazon Mechanical Turk. For region descriptions: workers draw bounding boxes and write descriptions, with subsequent workers encouraged to write descriptions not previously written, enforced using BLEU score thresholds. For objects: workers extract objects from descriptions and draw bounding boxes satisfying coverage and quality requirements. For attributes and relationships: workers add attributes to objects and connect pairs of objects with relationships based on region description text. For scene graphs: workers confirm co-referenced objects across region graphs. For QA pairs: workers write freeform QAs (8 pairs per image with at least 3 different W-types) and region-based QAs. All annotations go through verification using majority voting (3 workers, 2 must agree) or rapid judgments for objects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All Visual Genome data go through a verification stage. Majority voting involves three unique workers looking at each annotation and voting on whether it is factually correct; an annotation is added if at least two out of three workers verify it as correct. Rapid judgments (inspired by rapid serial visual processing) are used for object verification, providing an order of magnitude increase in speed over majority voting. Canonicalization mappings are verified by AMT workers who choose among 5 synset options without knowing which is the proposed mapping. Canonicalization achieved: objects 88.0% precision, 98.5% recall; attributes 85.7% precision, 95.9% recall; relationships 92.9% precision, 88.5% recall.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Average of 42 region descriptions per image, 21 objects per image, 16 attributes per image, 18 relationships per image, and 17 question-answer pairs per image. Each annotation is verified by 3 workers.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. Geographic distribution: United States 93.02%, Philippines 1.29%, Kenya 1.13%, India 0.94%, Russia 0.50%, Canada 0.47%, Others 2.65%. Age distribution: majority between 25 and 34 years old; youngest contributor was 18 years old, oldest was 68 years old. Gender: 54.15% male, 45.85% female.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) used to extract nouns automatically as suggestions for object extraction. Stanford NLP tools used to extract noun phrases for canonicalization. word2vec used for semantic analysis of descriptions. BLEU score used programmatically to enforce description diversity.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper refers to the 'first release' of the Visual Genome dataset. Further visualizations, API, and additional information are available at https://visualgenome.org. No explicit versioning, update schedule, or deprecation policy is described.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to enable cognitive computer vision tasks such as image description, question answering, and robotic interactions. It is intended to advance comprehensive scene understanding, enabling applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions. The dataset could help computers move from perceptual awareness to cognitive understanding of images.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as the top synsets show. The top 25 synsets include 'ski', 'ballplayer', and 'racket', indicating a bias towards images of people playing sports. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented in attribute descriptions due to a bias towards these sports in the image source. 93.02% of crowd workers contributed from the United States, which may introduce cultural and linguistic biases in annotations.
rai:dataLimitations: Canonicalization mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity. The dataset's object categories (17,000+) result in fewer examples per category compared to more focused datasets. Region descriptions have a maximum of 16 words, limiting detail. The QA baseline model shows that the top 1000 frequent answers cover only 64.1% of correct answers, indicating a long-tail distribution. Current models are unable to reason about complex images as demonstrated by low human accuracy scores (43.03% for region description generation).
rai:dataUseCases: Training and benchmarking computer vision models for: object detection, attribute prediction, relationship prediction/extraction, region description generation (dense image captioning), visual question answering, semantic image retrieval, scene graph generation, image understanding evaluation, action recognition, spatial reasoning, and knowledge base construction. The dataset is designed as a general-purpose representation of the visual world without bias toward a particular task.
